analysis.architecture_style: Java EE monolith (single EAR) on a WebLogic cluster with PL/SQL-heavy Oracle
analysis.summary: A 180k-line Java 7 / EJB 3.0 application with a JSF 1.2 UI, packaged as one EAR on a 4-node WebLogic 10.3.6 cluster and backed by a 1.2 TB Oracle 11g database with significant PL/SQL. Five integrations mix SOAP, SFTP, nightly Quartz ETL and LDAP. Because everything ships as one EAR, every release requires full re-validation, which drives the 6-month release cycle.

analysis.regulated_data: GCP records for ~120 active studies: subject enrolment (pseudonymised, GDPR special category), monitoring visit reports and Part 11 audit trails, with 25-year trial master file retention.

dimensions.rationale: Runtime, app server, database and OS are all out of support.
One 180k-LOC EAR; modules exist in code but deploy and validate together.
Clustered, but stateful JSF sessions and in-server batch jobs limit elasticity.
1.2 TB of Oracle with heavy PL/SQL; easiest path is managed Oracle, not an engine change.
Five integrations across SOAP, SFTP, batch ETL, SharePoint and LDAP, several vendor-owned.
GCP-critical with Part 11 audit trails, GDPR special category data, EU residency and 25-year retention.
evidence: EU subject data must stay in the EU

dimensions.rationale: Ant builds, no automated tests and a 6-month validated release cycle.

risks.title: Business logic locked in PL/SQL
risks.description: Core rules live in Oracle packages, so moving engines or extracting services can change validated behaviour.
risks.mitigation: Keep Oracle (managed) during replatform; extract services only behind characterisation tests.

risks.title: Audit trail continuity during data migration
risks.description: Inspection-ready audit trails must survive the migration complete and unaltered.
risks.mitigation: Validated migration with row counts and hash reconciliation of audit tables; QA review before go-live.

risks.title: Disruption to studies in database lock
risks.description: Two studies lock their databases in Q1; cutover then would jeopardise submissions.
risks.mitigation: Schedule cutover after Q1 lock; freeze changes for locking studies.

risks.title: EU subject data leaving the EU
risks.description: A single US-hosted deployment would breach residency commitments for EU subjects.
risks.mitigation: Deploy in an EU region with region-restricting guardrails; document transfers in the DPIA.

risks.title: Full re-validation for every release persists
risks.description: Without modular releases and automated tests, the cloud move alone will not shorten the 6-month cycle.
risks.mitigation: Adopt CSA, automate regression OQ, and validate extracted services independently.

risks.title: Container and Kubernetes skills gap
risks.description: The team knows WebLogic, not containers, EKS or IaC.
risks.mitigation: Pair with a partner for the first two waves; platform team owns golden pipelines.

risks.title: Oracle licensing on cloud
risks.description: Licence terms for Oracle on cloud can raise costs unexpectedly.
risks.mitigation: Use licence-included managed Oracle and right-size; plan a later move of new services to PostgreSQL.

risks.title: APAC site latency persists
risks.description: Moving the same server-rendered UI to one region keeps APAC slow.
risks.mitigation: Serve the new UI from a CDN and keep APIs chatty-free.

opportunities.title: Monthly instead of 6-monthly releases
opportunities.benefit: Independently validated services and automated OQ shrink the release cycle.

opportunities.title: Drop WebLogic licences
opportunities.benefit: Open-source Jakarta EE runtime on containers removes WebLogic licence cost.

opportunities.title: Faster experience for global sites
opportunities.benefit: A CDN-served UI improves performance in 25 countries.

opportunities.title: Inspection readiness on demand
opportunities.benefit: Centralised immutable audit logs make inspection evidence quick to produce.

opportunities.title: Self-service site onboarding
opportunities.benefit: Federated identity with MFA replaces manual site-user management.

plan.headline: Refactor TrialHub in about a year: first replatform the EAR to containers and managed Oracle on AWS, then strangle out site-management and monitoring services - validating each increment so releases drop from 6-monthly to monthly.

patterns.name: Strangler fig
patterns.why: Carve services out of the EAR one domain at a time, validating each small increment instead of the whole system.

patterns.name: Replatform to managed PaaS
patterns.why: Exit end-of-life WebLogic, Java 7 and Oracle 11g first while keeping PL/SQL logic intact.

patterns.name: API gateway facade
patterns.why: Decouples the EDC SOAP contract from EJBs and routes traffic between legacy and new services.

patterns.name: GxP landing zone
patterns.why: EU-resident, policy-guarded accounts with immutable audit logging for an inspected GCP system.

component_strategies.rationale: Replace JSF/RichFaces with a modern SPA served from a CDN for global sites, module by module.
Containerise the EAR on an open-source Jakarta EE runtime first, then extract site and monitoring services.
Licence-included managed Oracle keeps PL/SQL unchanged; new services get their own PostgreSQL schemas.
Move batch out of the app server into observable, retryable managed pipelines.
Vendor system stays; an API facade decouples its SOAP contract.
Vendor keeps SFTP; the endpoint moves to a managed service.
Out of scope; receives data from the new pipeline.
Federated identity with MFA for staff and external site users.
component_strategies.target_service: Amazon Cognito federated with corporate IdP

plan.target_summary: AWS in an EU region inside a GxP landing zone: a CDN-served SPA, the containerised core on Amazon EKS with extracted site and monitoring services, licence-included Amazon RDS for Oracle, an API Gateway facade for EDC, Transfer Family for IRT files, Step Functions/Glue for safety reconciliation, Cognito federation with MFA, and CloudTrail/CloudWatch for immutable audit logging.
